pos: n. (the Lombard Cistercian abbey of 1135, founded by Bernard of Clairvaux himself, named for his own house)
etymology: Italian Chiaravalle, the Italian form of Clairvaux, the clear valley, with Milanese for the city.
biblical_def: Chiaravalle Milanese south of Milan was founded in 1135 by Bernard of Clairvaux in person, during the journey on which he settled the papal schism in Lombardy, and he gave it the Italian form of his own abbey's name. It is distinct from Clairvaux in Champagne and from the other Italian Chiaravalle houses; this one is the Milanese daughter. The monks drained the marshes south of the city, the church was finished about 1221, and over the crossing rises the lantern tower the Milanese call the ciribiciaccola, a brick spire of stacked open loggias. The dictionary records Chiaravalle for the naming, because a daughter that takes its mother's name raises the question of headship, and Scripture answers it in a way that leaves no founder at the top. Christ is the head of the body and not Bernard, “And he is the head of the body, the church” (Col 1:18), and the appointment is reported as an act of the Father, “gave him to be the head over all things to the church” (Eph 1:22). The footing of the whole building admits no second name, “For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11), and the builder in the promise is Christ Himself, “upon this rock I will build my church” (Mat 16:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a filiation as the relation of a dependent house to its parent; an abbot as the superior of an abbey; a lantern in architecture is an open turret admitting light; headship as the state of being head; and a crossing would be the intersection of nave and transept.
webster_full: FILIATION, n. The relation of a son to a father; correlative to paternity; also, the relation of a dependent house to its parent.
ABBOT, n. The superior or governor of an abbey or monastery.
LANTERN, n. In architecture, a little dome raised over the roof of a building to give light, and to serve as a crowning.
HEADSHIP, n. Authority; chief place; the state of being head or chief.
TRANSEPT, n. In architecture, the transverse part of a church, crossing the nave at right angles.
scriptures: Col 1:18
And he is the head of the body, the church: who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead; that in all things he might have the preeminence.
Eph 1:22
And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church,
For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ.
And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
corruption_summary: Lombard Cistercian abbey of 1135 founded by Bernard of Clairvaux himself and named for his own house.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that headship in the church is not transmitted by founders, however great. Bernard planted this house himself and gave it his abbey's name, and the apostolic sentence on who heads the body leaves no room above it, “who is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead” (Col 1:18).

The live temptation is the veneration of a founder, which the Cistercians practised on Bernard and which every movement practises on its own. Scripture reports the headship as a gift from the Father and not an election by monks, “And hath put all things under his feet” (Eph 1:22); the footing bears one name only, “can no man lay than that is laid” (1Co 3:11); and the builder who guarantees the work is not the one who laid the first stone at Milan, “and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Mat 16:18).

“the head over all things to the church” (Eph 1:22) — a gift from the Father.
“which is Jesus Christ” (1Co 3:11) — the footing bears one name.

pos: n. (the Piedmontese Cistercian abbey of 1180, settled from Lucedio, long worked as a farm)
etymology: Italian rivalta, the high bank, with the river Scrivia.
biblical_def: Rivalta Scrivia in Piedmont was founded in 1180 and settled from Lucedio, and it spent most of its history doing what the order did best in the Po valley: diking a river, draining a plain and farming it. The church keeps a cycle of fifteenth-century frescoes. After the suppression the buildings passed into private hands and the estate has been worked as a farm ever since, so that the cloister stands among barns. The dictionary records Rivalta for the frank agriculture of it, because Scripture treats settled husbandry as a form of obedience and attaches a promise to it. The charge to a man who means to stay in a place is two plain verbs with a consequence, “Trust in the LORD, and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land” (Psa 37:3), and the proverb requires that he actually know what he keeps, “Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks” (Pro 27:23). The fruit of right dealing in such a place is quietness, “the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever” (Isa 32:17), and the law of the field does not negotiate, “whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Gal 6:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a dike as a bank to resist water; a barn as a covered building for grain; tillage as the preparing of land for seed; a farm as a tract of land leased or cultivated; and a steward as one entrusted with another's affairs.
webster_full: DIKE, n. A ditch; a channel for water made by digging; also, a mound of earth or stones raised to prevent inundation.
BARN, n. A covered building for securing grain, hay, flax, and other productions of the earth.
TILLAGE, n. The operation, practice or art of tilling or preparing land for seed, and keeping it free from weeds.
FARM, n. A tract of land leased on rent reserved; a portion of land devoted to agriculture.
STEWARD, n. A man employed to manage the domestic concerns, superintend the other servants, and collect the rents.
scriptures: Psa 37:3
Trust in the LORD, and do good; so shalt thou dwell in the land, and verily thou shalt be fed.
Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks, and look well to thy herds.
And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever.
Gal 6:7
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
corruption_summary: Piedmontese Cistercian abbey of 1180 settled from Lucedio, its cloister standing among the barns of a working farm.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that settled farming is a form of obedience with a promise attached. Rivalta diked the Scrivia and has been farmed for eight centuries, and the psalmist's charge to anyone who means to stay is two verbs and a result, “and verily thou shalt be fed” (Psa 37:3).

The live temptation is an absentee management that counts the yield and stops walking the fields, which is what the abbey became after the suppression and what it half was before. The proverb insists on real knowledge, “and look well to thy herds” (Pro 27:23); the promised fruit of right dealing is quiet rather than profit, “And the work of righteousness shall be peace” (Isa 32:17); and the law of the seed-bed applies to the manager as much as to the soil, “Be not deceived; God is not mocked” (Gal 6:7).

“Be thou diligent to know the state of thy flocks” (Pro 27:23) — management that keeps walking.
“quietness and assurance for ever” (Isa 32:17) — the promised fruit.

pos: n. (the Champagne abbey of 1115, the fourth elder daughter of Citeaux, mother of the German, Polish, Spanish and Hungarian branches, now almost wholly gone)
etymology: Latin Morimundus, read as the dying world, from mori and mundus.
biblical_def: Morimond in southern Champagne was founded in 1115 and was the last of the four elder daughters of Citeaux, after La Ferté, Pontigny and Clairvaux. Its line of descent is the largest of the four: through Morimond came the German houses, the Polish and Silesian houses, the Spanish and Portuguese houses, the Hungarian houses, and the military orders of Calatrava and Alcantara, some seven hundred foundations in all. The abbey was suppressed in the French Revolution and sold for its stone, and almost nothing of it stands: a gatehouse, a chapel, fragments in a wood. The dictionary records Morimond because the mother of seven hundred houses has less left of it than a Polish grange, which is the ordinary way of fruitfulness in Scripture. The sowing costs the sower, “They that sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psa 126:5), and the law that connects the two is stated as a law, “whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap” (Gal 6:7). The shortage in such work is never of ground, “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37), and what endures of a vanished house is not its masonry, “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines filiation as the relation of a dependent house to its parent; a mother-church as the church from which others spring; to suppress as to put down; a grange as a farm with its buildings; and progeny as offspring, descendants.
webster_full: FILIATION, n. The relation of a son to a father; also, the relation of a dependent house to its parent.
MOTHER-CHURCH, n. The church from which others have sprung; a metropolitan church.
SUPPRESS, v.t. To overpower and crush; to subdue; to destroy; to put an end to.
GRANGE, n. A farm, with the buildings, stables, &c.; a farm-house with the barns and other buildings.
PROGENY, n. Offspring; race; children; descendants of the human kind.
scriptures: They that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
Gal 6:7
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
Mat 9:37
Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;
Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
corruption_summary: The fourth elder daughter of Citeaux, 1115, ancestor of some seven hundred houses, now reduced to a gatehouse and fragments.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that fruitfulness and survival are different things. Morimond fathered seven hundred houses and has less standing than a Silesian grange, and the psalmist sets the cost of sowing before the joy of reaping without promising the sower a monument, “They that sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psa 126:5).

The live temptation is to measure a work by what is left of its headquarters. Scripture states the connection between sowing and reaping as a law that holds whatever becomes of the barn, “God is not mocked” (Gal 6:7); it locates the scarcity in workers rather than acres, “but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37); and it names the one thing that outlasts every foundation, “but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8).

pos: n. (the Catalan Cistercian abbey of 1151, royal pantheon of the Crown of Aragon, sacked in 1835 and since restored)
biblical_def: Poblet in Catalonia was founded in 1151 by Ramon Berenguer IV and settled from Fontfroide, and it became the royal pantheon of the Crown of Aragon: James I, Peter IV, John I, Martin, John II and others lie in alabaster tombs raised on arches across the transept. It was the richest monastery in Catalonia. In 1835, during the Spanish disentailment, a mob sacked it, broke open the tombs and burned the library, and it stood ruined for a century until Cistercians returned in 1940 and rebuilt; the royal remains were gathered and replaced in 1952. The dictionary records Poblet for the broken tombs, because a royal pantheon exists to make a claim about death that Scripture declines to grant. The question is left open by Job and not closed by alabaster, “If a man die, shall he live again?” (Job 14:14), and the sequence after death is fixed and admits no royal exception, “as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27). What is promised to the ruined place is rebuilding, “they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations” (Isa 61:4), and the agency in such a restoration is God's, “When the LORD shall build up Zion, he shall appear in his glory” (Psa 102:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pantheon in this use as a building containing the tombs of the illustrious; alabaster as a soft marble-like stone; disentailment would be the breaking of an entail; a tomb as a grave; and to sack as to plunder.
webster_full: PANTHEON, n. A temple or magnificent edifice dedicated to all the gods; a building containing memorials of the illustrious dead.
ALABASTER, n. A sub-variety of carbonate of lime, of a fine white color, used for vases and ornaments.
ENTAIL, n. An estate in fee entailed, or limited in descent to a particular heir or heirs.
TOMB, n. A grave; a sepulcher; a vault in the earth for the reception of the dead.
SACK, v.t. To storm; to take by storm and plunder; as, to sack a city.
scriptures: If a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come.
Heb 9:27
And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
Isa 61:4
And they shall build the old wastes, they shall raise up the former desolations, and they shall repair the waste cities, the desolations of many generations.
When the LORD shall build up Zion, he shall appear in his glory.
corruption_summary: Catalonia's richest Cistercian house, 1151, royal pantheon of Aragon, sacked in 1835 and rebuilt from 1940.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a tomb cannot make the claim a pantheon is built to make. Poblet's kings lay in alabaster above the floor of the transept until a mob broke them open in 1835, and the question Job leaves open is not answered by stone, “If a man die, shall he live again?” (Job 14:14).

The live temptation is the dynastic one, which is to buy with an endowment a standing at the judgment that nobody can buy. The sequence after death admits no royal exception, “but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27). What Scripture does promise a wrecked place is work, “And they shall build the old wastes” (Isa 61:4), and it assigns the agency in a restoration where the monks of 1940 would have assigned it, “he shall appear in his glory” (Psa 102:16).
roots_summary: Hebrew chalaph (H2498), to change, to pass on; Greek apokeimai (G0606), to be appointed; Hebrew churbah (H2723), a waste place; Hebrew bana (H1129), to build.

pos: n. (the Catalan Cistercian abbey of 1150, royal burial house of Peter III and James II, never re-monasticised)
biblical_def: Santes Creus in Catalonia was founded in 1150 and settled from Grandselve, and with Poblet it was one of the two great Cistercian houses of the principality. Peter III and James II of Aragon are buried there in canopied tombs, and its cloister, finished about 1340, is among the finest in Spain, with naturalistic foliage carving that breaks the order's own rule against ornament. It was suppressed in 1835 like Poblet, and unlike Poblet no community ever came back; the buildings are kept as a monument. The dictionary records Santes Creus for that permanent emptiness, and for the way Scripture handles a sanctuary with nobody in it. The lament is specific about what is missing, “The ways of Zion do mourn, because none come to the solemn feasts” (Lam 1:4). But the thing the patriarchs were looking for was never a building they could keep, “For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10), and the epistle applies that expectation to every Christian in every town, “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14). The city that finally stands is received and not built, “coming down from God out of heaven” (Rev 21:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cloister as a covered walk in a monastery; a canopy as a covering over a throne or tomb; foliage as leaves collectively, also leaf ornament; a monument as a memorial; and to suppress as to put an end to.
webster_full: CLOISTER, n. A monastery or nunnery; a covered passage or walk round a court, usually with a colonnade.
CANOPY, n. A covering over a throne, or over a bed; more generally, a covering over the head.
FOLIAGE, n. Leaves in general; as the foliage of trees; also, the representation of leaves in architecture.
MONUMENT, n. Any thing by which the memory of a person or of an event is preserved or perpetuated.
SUPPRESS, v.t. To overpower and crush; to subdue; to destroy; to put an end to.
scriptures: Lam 1:4
The ways of Zion do mourn, because none come to the solemn feasts: all her gates are desolate: her priests sigh, her virgins are afflicted, and she is in bitterness.
For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Rev 21:2
And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
corruption_summary: Catalan Cistercian abbey of 1150, royal burial house of Peter III and James II, suppressed in 1835 and never reoccupied.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an empty church is a loss and not an argument. Santes Creus has been a monument rather than a monastery for nearly two centuries, and the lament Scripture supplies for such a place names precisely what is absent, “all her gates are desolate” (Lam 1:4).

The live temptation is to treat the fabric as the hope, which a cloister that fine makes almost reasonable. The patriarchs are commended for looking past every building they could have kept, “whose builder and maker is God” (Heb 11:10); the expectation is extended to Christians in ordinary towns, “but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14); and the city that lasts descends rather than being raised, “I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem” (Rev 21:2).

pos: n. (the Castilian Cistercian nunnery of 1187 at Burgos, whose abbess exercised quasi-episcopal jurisdiction until 1873)
etymology: Spanish huelgas, fallow or resting ground, from holgar, to rest.
biblical_def: Las Huelgas outside Burgos was founded in 1187 by Alfonso VIII of Castile and his queen Eleanor of England, daughter of Henry II, as a Cistercian house for noble women, and it became a royal pantheon and one of the wealthiest convents in Europe. Its abbess held an extraordinary position: an exempt jurisdiction over more than fifty villages and a dozen parishes, the right to appoint and license the priests who served them, to hear cases in her own court, and to wear a mitre and carry a crozier. The jurisdiction was not abolished until a papal bull of 1873. The abbey also holds the earliest surviving Spanish polyphony. The dictionary honours the learning and the charity of the house and names the jurisdiction as the error. Teaching and ruling authority in the church are withheld from women by apostolic command, “But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man” (1Ti 2:12), and the office in question is described in terms that assume a man, “A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife” (1Ti 3:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a jurisdiction as legal authority, the extent of power; an abbess as the female superior of a nunnery; a crozier as a bishop's staff; exempt as free from a liability; and a benefice as an ecclesiastical living.
webster_full: JURISDICTION, n. The legal power or authority of doing justice in cases of complaint; the power of executing laws.
ABBESS, n. A female superior or governess of a nunnery or convent of nuns.
CROZIER, n. A bishop's crook or pastoral staff, a symbol of pastoral authority.
EXEMPT, adj. Free from any service, charge, burden, tax, duty, evil or requisition.
BENEFICE, n. In the middle ages, an estate in lands; in church use, an ecclesiastical living.
scriptures: But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Let your women keep silence in the churches: for it is not permitted unto them to speak; but they are commanded to be under obedience, as also saith the law.
corruption_summary: Castilian Cistercian nunnery of 1187 at Burgos whose abbess licensed priests and held her own court until 1873.
corruption_paragraphs: The abbess of Las Huelgas licensed preachers, confirmed the appointment of parish priests, heard matrimonial cases in her own court and bore a mitre, over a territory of some fifty villages, for nearly seven hundred years. The learning of the house was real and its charity was real, and the dictionary says so. The jurisdiction was an error, and the apostolic command on the point is not ambiguous, “nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence” (1Ti 2:12).

The corruption is not merely medieval, and it is now defended in the opposite direction. Egalitarian readings treat Las Huelgas as a precedent and a liberation, and progressive evangelical writers cite such cases as evidence that the New Testament restrictions were cultural. The texts do not read that way. The office of overseer is described in terms that presuppose a man, “the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour” (1Ti 3:2); the ordaining of elders is committed to Titus in the same register, “and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee” (Tit 1:5); and the apostolic rule for the assembly is stated as a command and grounded in the law, “Let your women keep silence in the churches” (1Co 14:34). None of this touches the dignity of the women themselves, who are joint heirs; it concerns one office.

pos: n. (the Leonese Cistercian abbey of about 1143, claimed as the first of the order in Spain, now a roofless ruin)
etymology: Spanish Moreruela, from a diminutive of mora, a mulberry or moorland.
biblical_def: Moreruela in Zamora was settled about 1143 from Clairvaux and is one of the two houses with a claim to be the first Cistercian abbey in Spain, the other being Fitero. Its church was built from about 1168 with an ambulatory and a ring of radiating chapels, a French plan unusual in Spain, and the ruin of that apse standing open in bare Castilian country is one of the most photographed monastic sites in the peninsula. It was suppressed in 1835 and the stone carted away for farm buildings. The dictionary records Moreruela for that apse, and for the care Scripture takes with ruins. Jeremiah quoted an older prophecy that even Zion would be farmland, “Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps” (Jer 26:18), so a carted-away abbey is not outside God's dealings. The lament over an emptied house is still a lament, “her priests sigh, her virgins are afflicted” (Lam 1:4). The promise over such sites is work, “And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places” (Isa 58:12), and the rebuke is reserved for those who panel their own houses while God's lies open, “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an apse in this sense as the vaulted recess at the end of a church; an ambulatory as a place to walk in; a chevet would be the eastern chapels; a quarry as a place where stones are dug; and to cart as to carry on a cart.
webster_full: APSIS, n. In architecture, an arched or vaulted recess at the end of a church or chapel.
AMBULATORY, n. A place to walk in; a part of a building appropriated to walking.
CHAPEL, n. A house for public worship; a place of worship subordinate to a parish church.
QUARRY, n. A place, cavern or pit where stones are dug from the earth, or separated from a large mass of rocks.
CART, v.t. To carry or convey on a cart; to expose in a cart.
scriptures: Micah the Morasthite prophesied in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and spake to all the people of Judah, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Zion shall be plowed like a field, and Jerusalem shall become heaps, and the mountain of the house as the high places of a forest.
Lam 1:4
The ways of Zion do mourn, because none come to the solemn feasts: all her gates are desolate: her priests sigh, her virgins are afflicted, and she is in bitterness.

And they that shall be of thee shall build the old waste places: thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations; and thou shalt be called, The repairer of the breach, The restorer of paths to dwell in.
Hag 1:4
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
corruption_summary: Leonese Cistercian abbey of about 1143, a rival claimant to be Spain's first, suppressed 1835 and quarried for farm buildings.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a carted-away abbey is inside the dealings of God and still worth grieving. Jeremiah quoted Micah to the effect that Zion itself would be ploughed, “Thus saith the LORD of hosts” (Jer 26:18), so the fate of Moreruela settles nothing about its merits.

The live temptation is the photograph, which turns a judgment into a composition. Lamentations keeps the tone at grief, “and she is in bitterness” (Lam 1:4); the word spoken over such sites proposes labour, “thou shalt raise up the foundations of many generations” (Isa 58:12); and the rebuke falls on those who finish their own houses first, “and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4).

pos: n. (the Aragonese Cistercian abbey of 1145, where Becquer wrote his Letters from my Cell in the emptied cloister)
etymology: Spanish Veruela, of uncertain origin, perhaps from a local water name.
biblical_def: Veruela under the Moncayo in Aragon was founded in 1145 by Pedro de Atarés and settled from Scala Dei in Gascony, one of the earliest Cistercian houses in the kingdom, with a walled precinct and a transitional church. It was suppressed in 1835. In the winter of 1863 and 1864 the poet Gustavo Adolfo Bécquer went there with his brother for his health and lived in the abandoned buildings, writing the Cartas desde mi celda, the Letters from my Cell, which are among the finest prose in Spanish and are the record of a man sitting in an emptied monastery thinking about mortality. Cistercians returned briefly in the twentieth century. The dictionary records Veruela for those letters, because they ask the question the building no longer answers. The psalmist states the measure of a man without softening it, “As for man, his days are as grass” (Psa 103:15), and Job puts the question itself and leaves it standing, “If a man die, shall he live again?” (Job 14:14). The expectation Scripture gives in place of a permanent cloister is frankly provisional, “For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14), and the posture it commends in the meantime is a waiting one, “It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lam 3:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cell as a small close apartment in a monastery; mortality as subjection to death; a precinct as a boundary; melancholy as a gloomy state of mind; and a hermitage as the habitation of a hermit.
webster_full: CELL, n. A small or close apartment, as in a prison or monastery; a cave; a small religious house.
MORTALITY, n. Subjection to death or the necessity of dying; also, death, actual or frequency of death.
PRECINCT, n. The limit, bound or exterior line encompassing a place; a territorial district.
MELANCHOLY, n. A gloomy state of mind, often a gloomy state that is of some continuance.
HERMITAGE, n. The habitation of a hermit; a cell or a dwelling in a solitary place.
scriptures: As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth.
If a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come.
For here have we no continuing city, but we seek one to come.
Lam 3:26
It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Aragonese Cistercian abbey of 1145 where Becquer wrote the Letters from my Cell in the buildings after the monks had gone.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that an emptied monastery still puts the question it was built to answer. Becquer spent a winter writing in Veruela's abandoned cells, and the psalmist's measure of a man is as blunt as anything in those letters, “as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth” (Psa 103:15).

The live temptation is the melancholy itself, which can become a resting place where Scripture offers a direction. Job asks the question and does not answer it from inside himself, “all the days of my appointed time will I wait” (Job 14:14); the epistle makes every present dwelling provisional rather than tragic, “but we seek one to come” (Heb 13:14); and the posture commended in the interval has an object, “and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD” (Lam 3:26).

pos: n. (the Navarrese Cistercian abbey of 1150, among the earliest in Spain, long known for its wine)
etymology: Spanish la oliva, the olive, from the tree in the abbey's arms.
biblical_def: La Oliva in Navarre was founded about 1150 by Garcia Ramirez and settled from L'Escale-Dieu in Gascony, among the first Cistercian houses in Spain, and its church of the later twelfth century is a textbook of the order's plain manner. The monks planted vines on the terraces above the Aragon river and the abbey's wine has been made there, with interruptions, for eight centuries; the community returned in 1927 and still works the vineyard. The dictionary records La Oliva for the vines, because the Lord took the vine for His own figure and placed the fruitfulness outside the vinedresser. The dependence is stated without qualification, “He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit” (Joh 15:5). The prophet's question to men labouring for the wrong vintage is pointed, “Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread?” (Isa 55:2). Honest work on a terrace is nevertheless promised a return, “In all labour there is profit” (Pro 14:23), and the prayer that fits a finished harvest is for establishing rather than praise, “establish thou the work of our hands upon us” (Psa 90:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a vine as the plant bearing grapes; a vintage as the produce of the vine for a season; a terrace as a raised level of earth; must as new wine; and a press as a machine for pressing.
webster_full: VINE, n. The plant that produces grapes, of the genus Vitis; also, a slender twining or trailing plant.
VINTAGE, n. The produce of the vine for the season; the grapes gathered, or the wine produced.
TERRACE, n. A raised level of earth, supported by a wall of masonry; a balcony or open gallery.
MUST, n. New wine; wine pressed from the grape but not fermented.
PRESS, n. An instrument or machine by which any body is squeezed, crushed or forced into a more compact form.
scriptures: Joh 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
Isa 55:2

Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
In all labour there is profit: but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury.
And let the beauty of the LORD our God be upon us: and establish thou the work of our hands upon us; yea, the work of our hands establish thou it.
corruption_summary: Navarrese Cistercian abbey of about 1150 whose monks have made wine on the terraces above the Aragon for eight centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the vinedresser is not the source of the vintage. La Oliva's monks have worked the same terraces for eight hundred years, and the Lord's use of their own trade puts the fruitfulness outside their hands, “for without me ye can do nothing” (Joh 15:5).

The live temptation is a trade that forgets its object, which is what the prophet asks about. The question is directed at the purchase rather than at the labour, “and your labour for that which satisfieth not?” (Isa 55:2); the proverb still grants honest work its return, “but the talk of the lips tendeth only to penury” (Pro 14:23); and the prayer over a gathered harvest asks for establishing rather than reputation, “yea, the work of our hands establish thou it” (Psa 90:17).

pos: n. (the Navarrese Cistercian abbey of 1140 whose abbot founded the military Order of Calatrava)
etymology: Spanish fitero, a boundary stone, from Latin fictorium, a marker.
biblical_def: Fitero in Navarre was settled in 1140 from Scala Dei and has the other claim, against Moreruela, to be the first Cistercian house in Spain. Its consequence is military. In 1158 the Templars gave up the defence of Calatrava, the fortress holding the road to Toledo, and Raymond, abbot of Fitero, with the knight Diego Velázquez, took it over, raised a force and held it; out of that undertaking grew the Order of Calatrava, the first Spanish military order, affiliated to Citeaux and governed under Cistercian visitation. Monks became the superiors of knights. The dictionary records Fitero as the point where the order crossed a line Scripture draws. The church's weapons are specified and the specification is exclusive, “For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God” (2Co 10:4), and the enemy named is not a Moorish garrison, “For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities” (Eph 6:12). Christ's word to Peter in the garden settles the method even for a disciple defending Him in person, “Put up again thy sword into his place” (Mat 26:52), and the agency in any real deliverance is named so that no army may claim it, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6). A lawful magistrate bearing arms is a different question, and the dictionary keeps it separate; an abbot raising a regiment is the thing named here.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a military order as a fraternity of knights; a commandery as a district under a commander; carnal as fleshly, pertaining to the body; warfare as military service, contest; and a castellan would be the governor of a castle.
webster_full: KNIGHT, n. Originally, a youth; afterward, a young man admitted to military rank with ceremonies.
COMMANDERY, n. A body of the knights of a military order, subordinate to the grand master.
CARNAL, adj. Fleshly; pertaining to flesh; not spiritual; opposed to spiritual.
WARFARE, n. Military service; military life; war; contest carried on by force of arms.
GARRISON, n. A body of troops stationed in a fort or fortified town.
scriptures: (For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
Eph 6:12
For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.
Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword.
Zec 4:6
Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.
corruption_summary: Navarrese Cistercian abbey of 1140 whose abbot took over the defence of Calatrava in 1158 and founded Spain's first military order.
corruption_paragraphs: In 1158 the abbot of Fitero accepted the garrison of a frontier fortress and began recruiting fighting men under monastic vows, and out of it came the Order of Calatrava, knights under Cistercian visitation. The dictionary grants the courage and the danger of the frontier and still names the step as a crossing. Paul specifies the church's armament, and the specification excludes a garrison, “but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4).

The corruption persists wherever the church takes up the sword in its own cause, whether in a crusading order or in a modern politics that treats the gospel as a programme to be imposed. The adversary named in the apostolic account is not a nation, “against the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Eph 6:12). Christ's word to Peter in the garden settles the method for a disciple defending even Him, “Put up again thy sword into his place” (Mat 26:52), and the agency in every real deliverance is named so that no army may claim it, “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6). A lawful magistrate bearing arms is another matter; an abbot raising a regiment is not.
